item.title: China's CERES-1 rocket launches new satellite from sea
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21
The CERES-1 Y8 carrier rocket carrying a new satellite blasts off from the waters near the city of Rizhao, east China's Shandong Province, Oct. 21, 2026. China launched a rocket from the ocean waters near the city of Rizhao in east China's Shandong Province on Wednesday, placing a new satellite into planned orbit. The CERES-1 Y8 carrier rocket blasted off at 11:39 a.m. (Beijing Time). The Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center carried out this offshore launch. (Photo by Wang Yan/Xinhua) RIZHAO, Shandong, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- China launched a rocket from the ocean waters near the city of Rizhao in east China's Shandong Province on Wednesday, placing a new satellite into designated orbit. The CERES-1 Y8 carrier rocket blasted off at 11:39 a.m. (Beijing Time). The Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center carried out this offshore launch. This new satellite will be mainly used for commercial remote sensing, providing services to the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, south China, and the low-latitude regions along the Maritime Silk Road, according to the Science and Technology Daily. The launch marked the seventh sea-based mission of the CERES-1 sea-launched carrier rocket series. As of now, the rocket's developer Galactic Energy has successfully conducted 23 orbital launches and placed a total of 90 commercial satellites into their designated orbits, the report noted. ■ The CERES-1 Y8 carrier rocket carrying a new satellite blasts off from the waters near the city of Rizhao, east China's Shandong Province, Oct. 21, 2026. item.title: Red tourism thrives in Liupan Mountain, China's Ningxia
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21
A drone photo taken on Sept. 18, 2026 shows a park commemorating the history of the Long March in Xiji County of Guyuan City, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. The Liupan Mountain runs through Guyuan City in Ningxia. In October 1935, Red Army soldiers crossed Liupan Mountain during the Long March, a historic military maneuver in modern Chinese history. It marks a key turning point in the history of the Long March. Now, the Liupan Mountain serves as a crucial ecological barrier and water resource conservation area, and local revolution-themed tourism is booming. Former revolutionary base areas in the region have drawn renewed interest from holidaymakers, with visits offering travelers a chance to learn about China's revolutionary history and reflect on the difficult years that helped shape modern China. item.title: World Insights: Cost-of-living protests highlight mounting economic, social pressures across Europe
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21
FRANKFURT, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Recent protests across Europe have brought social and economic strains into sharper focus, reflecting concerns that extend beyond prices to housing, incomes, public services and economic security. Governments face growing pressure to respond, but high debt, tight budgets and long-standing structural problems leave few quick or easy solutions. DEMONSTRATIONS ACROSS EUROPE Holding a cardboard sign reading "I am 81 and being evicted," retiree Maria Teresa Faleiro joined crowds in Lisbon protesting against soaring living costs and a deepening housing crisis. Despite never missing a payment on the 724-euro (813-U.S. dollar) monthly rent for the home she has lived in for 22 years, Faleiro faced eviction after her landlords refused to renew her lease. With nowhere else to go, she plans to appeal the court-ordered eviction, she said. Faleiro's struggle highlights the growing plight many pensioners in Portugal face in securing affordable housing. It also reflects a broader cost-of-living squeeze across Europe, where thousands have taken to the streets to protest rising housing, food, fuel and energy costs, even as headline inflation has eased. In France, protests that began with students demanding better school conditions and more teaching staff broadened into nationwide demonstrations over rising living costs and wider social grievances. Violence soon erupted on the sidelines of some rallies, with clashes, looting and arson reported in several cities. The historic city hall in Limoges was largely destroyed by fire. In Spain, more than 50 protests took place in Madrid and dozens of other Spanish cities on Oct. 3, demanding action on soaring rents, evictions and housing affordability after the government failed to pass emergency housing legislation. Elsewhere, protests in Italy and Belgium have reflected a broader mix of concerns over wages, prices, public services and fiscal tightening. In Milan, hundreds of black-clad demonstrators besieged Piazza del Duomo on Saturday, throwing firecrackers and bottles at police. At least four officers and 20 protesters were injured, while about 50 demonstrators were detained, according to the Italian news agency ANSA. ECONOMIC SECURITY UNDER STRAIN Beyond higher daily expenses, mounting financial pressures are fueling a broader sense of economic insecurity across the continent. Although inflation has eased from its peak, households continue to feel the cumulative impact of earlier price increases. The European Central Bank said food prices across euro-area countries were already 20 percent to 57 percent higher in August 2025 than at the end of 2019. Renewed energy pressures have added to the squeeze, with euro-area consumer energy inflation reaching 18.9 percent in September 2026, according to Eurostat. Housing pressures are particularly acute among young Europeans. Data released by Eurostat showed that in 2025, 26.9 percent of young people aged 15 to 29 in the European Union (EU) lived in overcrowded households. And 9.1 percent of them lived in households spending at least 40 percent of their disposable income on housing, way above the 7.7 percent recorded for the total population. Similar pressures are visible beyond the EU. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, property prices have risen by about 70 percent over the past five years, real estate agent Haris Kadic told the Federation News Agency (FENA). Local media also reported that some residents are borrowing money or relying on help from children and friends to cover basic expenses as housing and fuel costs rise. Emmanuel Conte, Milan's city councilor responsible for housing, told Italian daily la Repubblica this month that when people who keep a city running can no longer afford to live there, housing is no longer just a social and economic issue but a political one. Similarly, Jean Faniel, director general of Belgium's Centre for Socio-Political Research and Information, told Belgian media outlet BRUZZ that violence accompanying recent protests should be understood in the context of mounting social frustration. Faniel said peaceful demonstrations and violent confrontations are potentially interconnected rather than entirely separate phenomena, noting that successive austerity measures have placed mounting pressure on people's living conditions, generating frustration and resentment. STRUGGLE TO BALANCE FISCAL, SOCIAL NEEDS European governments have introduced housing, energy and income support, but high debt, aging populations and competing demands for defense and investment are narrowing their room for further action. As the European Commission expects France's deficit to reach 5.1 percent of GDP in 2026 and public debt to reach 118.1 percent, Oliver Nachtwey, a sociologist at the University of Basel, said the country's efforts to contain public debt through spending cuts leave governments with less room to invest in schools, teachers and other public services. Experts said the challenge is to reconcile fiscal discipline with social stability. Thomas Decreus, a scholar at the Department of Philosophy at Tilburg University, warned that weakening basic social protections could undermine social peace. "A budget must be sound, but social investments are also necessary," he said. Former Croatian Economy minister Ljubo Jurcic told Xinhua that price freezes can help contain immediate pressures, but governments must consider who ultimately bears the cost. In the longer run, stronger productivity and a better economic structure offer more sustainable protection for households, he said. While subsidies and price controls can provide relatively quick relief, expanding housing supply, improving public services and raising productivity can take years, analysts said. The challenge lies in how governments should respond to demands for immediate results while pursuing reforms that may take much longer to deliver tangible benefits, they said.■

item.title: One keystroke, a new career: AI reshapes China's film and TV industry
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21
BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- At a film and television industry park in Suzhou, east China's Jiangsu Province, Qin Wenshan sits glued to his computer screen, watching as visuals, sound effects, subtitles and special effects fall into place on a video timeline. With a single press of the Enter key, a team of AI agents springs into action, analyzing the script, designing characters and building scenes frame by frame. Qin entered the field in late 2023, after stumbling across AI-generated content (AIGC), leading him to experiment with AI video production in his spare time. Before that, he had worked as a safety management officer in the local rail transit sector. After his short-video series racked up hundreds of millions of views, Qin turned his hobby into a business, putting together a team focused on AI-powered content production. His journey offers a glimpse into a broader transformation sweeping China's film and TV industry, where advances in AIGC video technology are changing not only how content is made, but also who can make it and at what cost. PRODUCTION GETS A RESHUFFLE Making a film or TV series used to require large teams of screenwriters, directors, cinematographers, production designers, editors, and visual effects artists, with all hands on deck. A crew could range from a few dozen people to several hundred and beyond. The bigger the spectacle, the higher the bill. Productions involving animation, sci-fi or fantasy often come with high costs, particularly when they feature complex settings and elaborate visual effects. AI is changing the math. Qin's team put AI to work on "PandaPawz," a sci-fi animated short featuring futuristic settings and intense fight scenes, completing the film in just 28 days at a cost of around 30,000 yuan (about 4,464 U.S. dollars). Industry data shows that AI can dramatically shorten production schedules, cutting timelines that once stretched over months or even years to just days. Some short-form drama episodes can now be produced in just hours, while efficiency in visual effects and previsualization has increased threefold to tenfold. Yet AI's role goes far beyond generating images. Li Nan, a creator of AI-generated animated dramas, said the process begins with refining the story outline and developing detailed storyboards. AI tools then generate frames with consistent visual styles and character designs, which are turned into videos and combined with AI voice-overs and automated editing to create finished episodes. This streamlined workflow enables small teams to handle work that once required extensive collaboration. In April, Li formed a two-person team dedicated to AI-generated animated dramas. Since then, its account has amassed more than 140,000 followers. "Film and TV production used to be a massive team effort. Now, one person can do the work of an entire department, with AI as the backbone," Qin said. GROWING DEMAND The rapid expansion of AI-generated dramas is evident in both output figures and market projections. Official data released in September showed that 430,000 micro-dramas had been released nationwide in the first eight months of this year -- 13 times the total for all of 2025 -- with AI-made productions accounting for more than 90 percent. The country now has more than 800 million viewers of micro-dramas -- series whose episodes run for less than 20 minutes. The market was worth more than 100 billion yuan in 2025. The demand is expected to grow further. According to a report by DataEye, an industry data platform, China's AI-generated drama and animation market alone is projected to reach 40 billion yuan in 2026, a year-on-year increase of 138 percent. The boom, however, also raises questions about content quality and the protection of rights and interests. The National Radio and Television Administration (NRTA) has acknowledged that AI is creating new opportunities for creative expression and more cost-efficient micro-drama production, while also highlighting the challenges the technology poses. "Our position is clear: live-action dramas are the mainstay of quality productions and should receive strong support," said Wang Xiaoliang, an official with the NRTA, at a September news conference on the development of radio, television, and the online audio and video sector over the next five years. At the same time, the administration said it will guide and regulate the innovative use of AI across the entire production process of audiovisual content in the coming years. For industry leaders, the future may lie not in choosing between AI and traditional filmmaking, but in combining the two. Gong Yu, founder and CEO of iQIYI, a leading online entertainment platform, believes the use of AI in film and drama production will be common in the future, and that a hybrid approach combining live-action filming with AI may be the way forward. The Chinese company is already exploring the potential of AI in longer productions. In July, it premiered "Mystic Tales: The Spider Lady's Vendetta," an AIGC internet feature film running over 60 minutes, which brings Chinese supernatural folklore to life, on both its domestic and international platforms. Recently, it unveiled a trailer for "Immortals Over Mortal Love," its first full-length, multi-season drama combining AI filmmaking with live-action performances by professional actors. The first season of the series is produced on NadouPro, the company's film and TV production platform empowered by large models. The move toward AI-generated long-form dramas signals a new stage in the technology's development, industry insider Hu Jie said, adding that these productions may face a tougher test of their storytelling, visual quality and ability to strike an emotional chord with audiences. ■

item.title: Mainland denounces Taiwan authorities for hindering cross-Strait exchanges
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21
BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday criticized the Taiwan authorities for barring relevant people on the island from attending the commemorative event held on the mainland marking the 160th anniversary of the birth of Sun Yat-sen. Sun, a founding figure of the Chinese Kuomintang (KMT) and a revered revolutionary leader who played a pivotal role in overthrowing imperial rule in China, died in 1925 in Beijing. His remains rest at the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum in Nanjing, east China's Jiangsu Province. Zhang Han, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, noted that the grand commemoration of Sun's legacy is intended to inherit and carry forward his noble spirit of upholding national unity and striving for national rejuvenation. She stressed that the move by Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities to obstruct cross-Strait exchanges and suppress Taiwan compatriots fully exposes their vicious intentions of betraying the nation and history, seeking to split the country, and stoking confrontation across the Taiwan Strait. The Taiwan question stems from China's civil war fought between the forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the KMT about eight decades ago. In 1949, the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, and the People's Republic of China was founded under the leadership of the CPC. The unresolved civil war, combined with foreign interference, has kept the two sides of the Taiwan Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation. However, the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed. Recently, Taiwan authorities also rejected an application by mainland actor Zhang Linghe to visit the island for cultural exchanges. Zhang Han criticized this decision as politically motivated, saying it undermined cross-Strait cultural exchanges and ran counter to the desire of people on both sides for closer ties. She urged the DPP authorities to respect this shared desire, abandon political maneuvering, lift unreasonable restrictions and facilitate cultural exchanges across the Strait. The spokesperson also commented on a recent incident involving singer Jay Chou from Taiwan, who reposted and liked a video in which he was introduced as a "Chinese singer." The move drew praise from some internet users on both sides of the Strait, while pro-DPP figures criticized it. Zhang stressed that people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait are all Chinese. She slammed "Taiwan independence" secessionists for opposing the close bonds between people across the Strait and seeking to use political means to restrict legitimate expression by Taiwan residents, saying such actions reflected malicious intent and lacked public support. ■

item.title: China-Central Asia cooperation boosts SCO development
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21
DUSHANBE, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- During his just-concluded official visits to Uzbekistan and Tajikistan and attendance at the 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (Prime Ministers) of Member States of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), Chinese Premier Li Qiang called for closer cooperation with the two Central Asian countries and greater development of the SCO. In recent years, China has deepened practical cooperation with Central Asian countries and injected fresh momentum into development of the SCO by enhancing connectivity, trade and exchanges in various fields. Analysts say these efforts will contribute to common prosperity and high-quality development in the region and beyond. CONNECTIVITY BRINGS OPPORTUNITY Enhancing connectivity between China and the landlocked countries of Central Asia is key to promoting development in the region and beyond. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, now under construction, is a prime example of this effort. In recent years, the railway project has remained high on the agenda of leaders of the countries involved. Most recently, during Li's official visit to Uzbekistan, the two sides pledged to advance the railway's high-quality construction. The railway, launched at the end of 2024, is a flagship project of the Belt and Road Initiative, serving as a strategic link between China and Central Asia. The route will begin in Kashgar in northwest China and pass through the mountainous terrain of Kyrgyzstan to reach Uzbekistan. High-quality construction and efficient operation of the railway will set a valuable example for countries across the region and beyond, said Kubanychbek Taabaldiev, a professor at Ala-Too International University in Bishkek. "It has the potential to change the economic geography of Central Asia and transform Kyrgyzstan from a country located between major markets into an important link between China, Central Asia, and further on to European and Middle Eastern destinations," Taabaldiev said. Beyond railway and road construction, the strengthening of transport cooperation between China and Central Asian countries also encompasses facilitating customs clearance at borders, digitizing transport permits and other efficiency-enhancing measures. Better connectivity has created new development opportunities for the region, boosting trade and exchanges in various fields. Ulugbek Shermatov, chairman of the Committee on International Affairs, Defence and Security of the Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis of Uzbekistan, noted that the creation of new transport arteries "not only expands economic opportunities, but also forms a solid material foundation for long-term interdependence and peaceful cooperation in the region." This demonstrates China's commitment to developing friendly relations with neighboring states and promoting Belt and Road cooperation, Shermatov said. PRACTICAL COOPERATION BEARS FRUIT From trade and agriculture to cutting-edge technological innovation, practical cooperation between China and Central Asia has been a driving force behind regional growth and, more broadly, the development of the SCO as a whole. Trade figures speak to the robust momentum in cooperation. China's trade with five Central Asian countries topped 100 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, hitting a record high. Meanwhile, trade structure continues to improve, with more Central Asian products entering the Chinese market. "Stability in the region is inextricably linked with trade and economic development. The growth of the total trade turnover of Central Asian countries with China ... clearly demonstrates China's importance in ensuring stability in our region," said Shermatov. Building on traditional merchandise trade, both sides are further expanding cooperation in digital trade, agriculture, energy, manufacturing, as well as scientific and technological innovation. Take energy cooperation as an example. Cooperation has gradually expanded from traditional oil and gas to clean energy and related technologies. At the Second China-Central Asia Summit in Astana, Kazakhstan last year, China and the five Central Asian nations pledged to support the establishment of a China-Central Asia energy development partnership to expand cooperation across the entire energy industry chains. The countries also affirmed their commitment to promoting technological and talent exchanges and cooperation in areas such as the management and development of desertified and saline-alkali lands. "China possesses rich technical expertise in renewable energy, electric mobility, digital infrastructure, telecommunications, artificial intelligence (AI) and industrial automation," said Mukhtor Umarov, chairman of the Economic Assembly of Uzbekistan. At the broader SCO level, the establishment and development of cooperation platforms between China and other SCO members in emerging fields "have opened new avenues for countries in the region -- shifting the focus from simply purchasing equipment toward technology localization, joint R&D, engineer cultivation and the buildout of new production capacities," Umarov said. SCO DEVELOPMENT STRENGTHENED Leaders of China and Central Asian nations, together with their SCO colleagues, reaffirmed stronger cooperation within the SCO framework at the just-concluded 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (Prime Ministers) of Member States of the SCO in the Tajik capital of Dushanbe. China's coordination with Central Asia will help promote the high-quality development of the SCO by strengthening the foundation for regional security, expanding economic cooperation and connectivity, and cementing mutual trust among member states. These efforts will further enhance the SCO's role in safeguarding regional security, promoting common development and improving global governance, experts said. "In my view, the most prominent feature of China's current contribution to the development of the SCO lies in its tight integration of strategic concepts, multilateral rules and concrete development tools," said Uzbek expert Umarov. "Against the backdrop of intensifying geoeconomic fragmentation, increasing trade restrictions, and chronic shortages of long-term financing, SCO member states urgently need predictable rules and institutions to mitigate risks faced by enterprises," he said. China has been a key contributor to the SCO's evolution. At the Tianjin Summit last year, a milestone in the SCO's development, China and other member states jointly formulated a development strategy for the organization for the next decade and action plans to promote high-quality development. Since the Tianjin Summit, a number of cooperation platforms have been launched, covering green industry, digital economy, scientific and technological innovation, energy, education and AI. At the Bishkek Summit earlier this year, China brought more initiatives and projects supporting the SCO's development, including the establishment of a China-SCO port economic cooperation center in Tianjin, the launch of an international AI application cooperation center, and the training of more green industry professionals. The SCO's international significance is "determined not only by its geographical reach or the combined potential of its member states, but also by its ability to translate political agreements into functioning mechanisms for security, economic cooperation, and diplomatic coordination," said Guzel Maitdinova, director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University. "Looking ahead, linking SCO economic initiatives with national development strategies, China's Belt and Road Initiative, and the programs of international financial institutions could play a particularly important role," Maitdinova added. Shermatov, meanwhile, offered an Uzbek perspective: "This is precisely how we see the responsibility of China and Uzbekistan for the future of the SCO -- to preserve the Shanghai Spirit while simultaneously adapting the organization to new global realities." ■

item.title: China's Long March legacy endures from trek to tech
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21
BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- One of the most visible legacies of the Red Army's Long March, a roughly 12,500-km military odyssey that ended 90 years ago, may well be an active rocket family that bears the same name. Among the world's busiest launch vehicles, China's Long March rockets have for more than half a century carried satellites, crewed spacecraft and scientific probes into orbit and beyond, helping open the country's path to space. This name for the rocket was suggested by several pioneers of China's aerospace industry. "It meant that the development of the rockets would overcome all difficulties and achieve victory, just as the Red Army had done during the Long March," said Han Houjian, a general designer of the Long March-1 rocket, which made its maiden flight in 1970. On April 24, 1970, the Long March-1 lifted off carrying Dongfanghong-1, China's first satellite, into orbit. Since then, this rocket family has grown into a diverse fleet of launch vehicles with increasing payload capabilities. As of October 10, 2026, it had completed 671 orbital launches. The journey behind these Chinese rockets echoes that of the Red Army: both were marked by immense hardships, determined perseverance, and the resolve to press ahead against the odds. In October 1934, the Communist Party of China (CPC) was forced to retreat from the Central Soviet Area in east China's Jiangxi Province and move northwest after enduring a series of encirclement campaigns by rival forces of the Kuomintang party. The CPC-led Red Army broke through enemy blockades, crossed rugged terrain, and endured fierce battles and immense hardship. Tens of thousands of soldiers lost their lives along the way. Few people represent the connection between these two journeys better than Sun Jixian. During the Long March, Sun, as a Red Army officer, led his men across a major river under enemy fire, helping the Red Army break through a dangerous bottleneck in 1935. More than a decade later, after the founding of the People's Republic of China, he took on a different mission -- building the country's first missile and satellite launch site in the remote Gobi Desert. His team battled sandstorms, drank alkaline water, lived in tents and caves, and transferred equipment by hand across the barren landscape. "I remember once when my father returned from the desert, he reached into his coat pocket to look for candies for me, but what he touched was a handful of rough, cold sand," recalled Sun Dongning, his 75-year-old son. In the 1960s, when China began developing its first rocket, the country had a weak industrial base and was cut off from access to many key foreign technologies. Scientists performed calculations using hand-cranked computing machines and worked day and night in poor workshops. China's first nuclear-powered submarine emerged from similarly difficult conditions and relied on technological self-reliance to overcome obstacles. Commissioned on Aug. 1, 1974, it was also named Long March-1. Subsequent generations of Chinese nuclear submarines have continued to carry the Long March name. The epic trek's legacy has since spread across military and technology sectors. Naval vessels such as Zunyi and Chishui bear the names of places associated with the historic march. Loongson, a major Chinese chipmaker, also gave two generations of its chips the project codes CZ70 and CZ80 in 2006 and 2016, respectively. CZ stands for Changzheng, the Chinese name for the Long March. For Chinese scientists and engineers, the legacy is not simply a name but a determination to persevere in facing daunting challenges, maintain faith in eventual success, and grow more resilient with every setback. Long Lehao, a leading Chinese rocket designer, cited the launch failure of Long March-3B as an example. As the rocket's first chief designer and chief commander, Long recalled that his hair "turned white overnight." "There was no time to think about personal honor or disgrace. I threw myself into the new battle of tracing faults," Long recalled at a recent press conference. After 30 days and nights of continuous work, his team identified the cause of the failure. Some 551 days later, the Long March-3B successfully delivered its payloads into orbit. The Long March-5, designed to carry lunar and Mars probes, suffered a rare setback when its second flight failed in 2017. The failure marked the darkest chapter in this rocket's development. The research team carried out painstaking reviews and repeated trials to resolve the technical problem. On Dec. 27, 2019, the rocket completed a successful third flight and subsequently launched several spacecraft, including the Chang'e-6 probe for a far-side lunar sample-return mission. And the journey continues. In July 2026, the Long March-10B completed China's first controlled recovery of a rocket's first stage, marking a step forward in reusable launch technology. Meanwhile, development of rockets with greater capability is being accelerated. China aims to land astronauts on the moon before 2030 and launch a Mars sample-return mission around 2028. Additionally, it is pursuing the broader goal of becoming an innovative nation and a world-class science and technology power. For generations of Chinese researchers, the Long March is a journey that never ends. From rugged trails to the frontiers of technology, its legacy is continuing to inspire further exploration and innovation. ■

item.title: Xi congratulates Central Institute of Socialism on 70th founding anniversary
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-20
BEIJING, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday sent a congratulatory letter to the Central Institute of Socialism, celebrating its 70th founding anniversary. In the letter, Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, praised the institute for training a large number of non-CPC representatives who share the CPC's ideals and work in unity toward common goals, and for making important contributions to consolidating and developing the patriotic united front over the past 70 years. He encouraged the institute to continue strengthening political training, building broad political consensus, and improving the quality of its teaching and research as well as its governance capacity. Xi called on the institute to play a greater role in training talent for the united front, conducting theoretical research and promoting principles and policies, so as to better serve the overall work of the CPC and the country. The congratulatory letter was read out at a gathering marking the institute's anniversary in Beijing on Tuesday. Wang Huning, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, addressed the event. Wang said Xi's congratulatory message fully recognized the institute's achievements and contributions, and set out directions and requirements for strengthening the institute and enhancing its role. Wang said the CPC Central Committee has consistently supported the development of the institute over the past 70 years. He called for stronger political consensus-building through sustained political training, higher-quality education to better train personnel for the united front, and continued efforts to enforce strict management of the institute. The institute was established on Oct. 15, 1956. Over the past seven decades, it has made significant contributions to upholding and improving the system of multiparty cooperation under the leadership of the CPC and to consolidating and strengthening the patriotic united front. ■ Wang Huning, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, addresses a gathering marking the 70th founding anniversary of the Central Institute of Socialism in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 20, 2026. Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, on Tuesday sent a congratulatory letter to the Central Institute of Socialism, celebrating its 70th founding anniversary. The congratulatory letter was read out at the gathering marking the institute's anniversary in Beijing. (Xinhua/Liu Bin)
